title: Long/Short Equity
summary: The most common hedge fund strategy: what actually drives its returns, how exposure is measured, and the specific ways it breaks.

lesson.body:
[[long-short-equity|Long/short equity]] is the largest strategy by asset count in the [[hedge-fund]] universe and the one you will meet first. The manager buys stocks they expect to do well — [[long-position|long positions]] — and simultaneously sells borrowed stocks they expect to do badly, via [[short-selling]].

That second leg is the entire point. A traditional equity fund can only express "this company is good". A long/short manager can also express "this company is bad", and can profit from being right about it. Two ways to add value instead of one, and a lever for controlling how much of the overall market's movement they are exposed to.

In practice most long/short equity managers stay net long. They are not trying to eliminate market exposure — they are trying to be paid for stock selection *on top of* a reduced dose of it.

Here is the thing that takes a while to feel properly: shorting is not the mirror image of going long.

When you buy a stock, the worst case is that it goes to zero and you lose what you put in. Your loss is capped and your position shrinks as it goes against you. When you short a stock, there is no ceiling on the price. Your loss is theoretically unlimited and — worse — the position *grows* as it moves against you. A short that doubles goes from 3% of your book to 6% while simultaneously costing you money.

So the payoff is asymmetric in the uncomfortable direction: losses compound into larger positions, and gains shrink into smaller ones. This single mechanical fact explains most of what is distinctive about the strategy — why short books are usually more diversified than long books, why position sizing discipline matters more than stock picking skill on the short side, and why a manager can be right about a company's fundamentals and still be forced out of the trade before being proved right.

You cannot discuss this strategy without two numbers, both expressed as a percentage of the fund's [[net-asset-value]].

**[[net-exposure]]** is longs minus shorts. It answers: how much market am I actually carrying? A fund 130% long and 60% short has 70% net exposure, so it should behave roughly like 70 cents of equity market for every dollar of capital.

**[[gross-exposure]]** is longs plus shorts. It answers: how much total position am I running? That same fund has 190% gross — nearly two dollars of stock working for every dollar of capital.

Two funds can have identical net exposure and behave nothing alike. A fund at 70% net via 85% long and 15% short is a mildly hedged long-only fund. A fund at 70% net via 130% long and 60% short is doing something far more active, with more ways to be right and more ways to be wrong. **Net tells you about market risk; gross tells you about selection risk and how hard the portfolio is working.**

lesson.plainReading: Net exposure is long percentage minus short percentage; gross exposure is long percentage plus short percentage. Both are quoted as a percentage of net asset value, and shorts enter as a positive number in the gross calculation even though they are short positions.

variables.meaning: long positions as a percentage of [[net-asset-value]]
short positions as a percentage of [[net-asset-value]], stated as a positive number

lesson.body: This worked decomposition is the single most useful thing in this topic. A fund runs 130% long and 60% short. Over the period, its long book returns +14%, the stocks it is short return +6%, and the broad equity market returns +10%.
walkthrough: **Long leg P&L.** 130% of NAV earning 14% contributes 1.30 x 14% = **+18.2%**.
**Short leg P&L.** The shorted stocks *rose* 6%, which costs a short seller. 60% of NAV short, losing 6%, contributes -0.60 x 6% = **-3.6%**.

**Now split it into market and skill.** With 70% [[net-exposure]] and a market up 10%, roughly 0.70 x 10% = **+7.0%** came simply from being net long. That is [[beta]] — the manager was paid for carrying market risk, which the investor could have bought far more cheaply.

**The residual is selection.** 14.6% - 7.0% = **+7.6%**, which is the candidate for [[alpha]]. Verify it from the other direction: longs beat the market by 4pp on 130% exposure = +5.2%; the shorts rose 6% against a market up 10%, so they lagged by 4pp, and being short something that lagged by 4pp on 60% exposure = +2.4%. Together, 5.2% + 2.4% = **+7.6%**. The two routes agree.

**Read the result properly.** Both legs worked: the longs outperformed and the shorts underperformed. That is a genuinely good period, and note it did *not* require the shorts to fall — they rose 6% and still contributed positively to skill, because they rose less than the market.

lesson.body:
Unpack a long/short equity return and you find four things, only one of which you are paying fees for.

1. **Market [[beta]]** — net exposure multiplied by the market's return. Real money, but cheaply replicable with an index fund.
2. **[[factor-exposure]]** — persistent tilts toward things like small caps, growth, momentum or quality. Also real money, also largely replicable, and often unintentional.
3. **Stock selection** — the genuine [[alpha]] candidate. Longs beating their comparables and shorts lagging theirs.
4. **Financing and [[short-rebate]]** — the interest earned on short sale proceeds, minus [[stock-borrow]] costs and margin interest. Small in a low-rate world; meaningful when short rates are high.

The whole discipline of evaluating one of these managers is separating item 3 from items 1 and 2. A manager who returned 18% in a year the market rose 25% at 70% net exposure has not obviously demonstrated anything.

lesson.caption: What helps and what hurts
rows: Wide gaps between winners and losers give selection something to bite on. Dispersion, not direction, is the strategy's raw material.
Net long exposure earns beta while shorts still have room to lag.
Everything rises, including the shorts. The lowest-quality names often rise most, so the short book bleeds precisely when it should protect.
Stocks move together on macro news, so fundamental differences stop being paid. Selection skill is drowned out.
If longs and shorts share an unintended factor tilt, both legs lose at once. The hedge stops hedging exactly when it is needed.

lesson.body:
**A long/short equity fund is not a market neutral fund.** The names sound similar and the distinction is not cosmetic.

[[equity-market-neutral]] managers deliberately hold net exposure near zero, so their return should be nearly independent of market direction. A typical long/short equity manager runs meaningfully net long — often 30% to 70% — and will therefore make money in rising markets and lose it in falling ones, largely regardless of stock picking.

If you are told a fund is "hedged" and you take that to mean "protected", you will be surprised in the first serious selloff. The right question is never "is it hedged?" but "what is the net exposure, and how much does it move?"

Every strategy has characteristic failure modes, and you should be able to name these without notes.

**[[short-squeeze]].** A heavily shorted stock rises sharply, forcing shorts to buy to close, which pushes it higher, which forces more buying. Losses on the short book accelerate non-linearly, and the position grows as it goes wrong.

**[[crowded-trade|Crowding]].** When many managers hold the same longs and the same shorts, they are effectively one giant position. If one large holder is forced to unwind, everyone's book moves against them simultaneously. Crowding turns independent-looking positions into a single correlated risk.

**Excessive [[gross-exposure]].** High gross magnifies everything, including mistakes. At 300% gross, a 5% adverse move across the book is a 15% hit to capital. Gross is where leverage hides in this strategy — a fund can look conservatively positioned on net exposure while running an enormous gross book.

**Unintended [[factor-exposure]].** The manager believes they are running a stock-selection book. In reality the longs are all high-growth and the shorts are all value. When that factor reverses, both legs lose together and the hedge provides nothing.

**[[stock-borrow]] recall and [[margin-call|margin calls]].** The lender of a borrowed share can demand it back, forcing the manager to close a short at the worst moment. Simultaneously, the [[prime-broker]] can raise margin requirements. Both tend to happen in stressed markets, and both force [[deleveraging]] — selling longs and buying back shorts into a market already moving against you. This is the mechanism that turns a bad month into a terminal one.

When a long/short equity manager's report crosses your desk, a short list of questions does most of the work.

**Net exposure over time, not just today.** A single number is nearly useless. Plot it. A manager whose net exposure swings from 20% to 90% is making macro timing calls, whether or not they describe themselves that way — and should be evaluated on that skill too.

**Gross exposure alongside it.** Rising gross with flat net means the manager is adding conviction on both sides. Rising gross with rising net means they are simply adding risk.

**[[performance-attribution]], long versus short.** Ask for it separately. Plenty of managers have a good long book and a short book that has cost them money every year — which is a long-only fund with an expensive hedge attached, and should be priced as such.

**Short book concentration and borrow.** A concentrated short book in hard-to-borrow small caps is a different risk profile from a diversified short book in liquid large caps, however similar the headline exposures look.

**[[drawdown]] behaviour.** When did the worst months happen, and what was the market doing? Losses in a falling market are consistent with net long exposure and are forgivable. Large losses in a *rising* market usually mean the short book failed, and that is the more troubling pattern — it suggests the manager was wrong about the thing they are paid to be right about.

items: Net exposure tells you about market risk; gross exposure tells you about selection risk and leverage. Always look at both, and over time rather than at a point.
Shorting is asymmetric: losses are uncapped and the position grows as it moves against you. That single fact shapes how short books are constructed.
Separate beta and factor tilts from genuine stock selection before crediting a manager with alpha.
The characteristic failure modes are squeezes, crowding, excessive gross, unintended factor tilts, and forced deleveraging from borrow recall or margin calls.

questions.stem: A fund is 118% long and 43% short, both as a percentage of net asset value. What is its net exposure, in percent?
questions.explanation: [[net-exposure]] = longs - shorts = 118% - 43% = 75%. The fund should behave roughly like 75 cents of equity market exposure per dollar of capital, before any stock selection effects.

questions.stem: The same fund is 118% long and 43% short. What is its gross exposure, in percent?
questions.explanation: [[gross-exposure]] = longs + shorts = 118% + 43% = 161%. Shorts count as a positive contribution to gross because they represent real positions carrying real risk, regardless of direction. Gross is where leverage hides in this strategy.

questions.stem: Fund X is 85% long and 15% short. Fund Y is 130% long and 60% short. What is the most useful thing to say about them?
choices: They carry similar market exposure, but Fund Y is running far more total position and therefore far more selection risk
They are effectively the same strategy, since both have 70% net exposure
Fund X is riskier, because it is less hedged
Fund Y has lower market risk, because it has a larger short book
rationales: Correct. Both are at 70% net, so both carry similar market risk. But Fund Y's gross of 190% against Fund X's 100% means Y is running nearly twice the total position — many more bets, more financing cost, and much more exposure to being wrong about individual names.
Identical net exposure is exactly the trap. Net alone cannot distinguish a mildly hedged long-only fund from an aggressively positioned one. That is precisely why gross is quoted alongside it.
Fund X has the *smaller* gross book and no more market exposure than Y, so on both measures it is carrying less risk, not more.
The larger short book is offset by a larger long book. Net exposure is identical at 70%, so market risk is comparable — the bigger short book buys Y more selection risk, not less market risk.
questions.explanation: Net and gross answer different questions and you need both. Net: how much market am I carrying? Gross: how hard is the portfolio working, and how much leverage is in it? Reporting one without the other is a genuine information gap.

questions.stem: A fund is 120% long and 50% short. Over the quarter its long book returns +8% and the stocks it is short return -4%. Ignoring fees and financing, what is the fund's gross return, in percent?
questions.inputHint: Answer in percent, to 1 decimal place. Use a minus sign if negative.
questions.explanation: Long leg: 1.20 x 8% = +9.6%. Short leg: the shorted stocks fell 4%, which is a gain for a short seller, so -0.50 x -4% = +2.0%. Total = +11.6%. Both legs worked — the mark of a genuinely good period. The most common error is dropping a sign on the short leg and getting +7.6%.

questions.stem: A manager returned +18% for the year. The equity market returned +25%. Average net exposure was 70%. What is the fairest initial read?
choices: Strong performance, since +18% is a good absolute return
Roughly in line with what net exposure alone would have delivered, so no clear evidence of stock selection skill
Clear evidence of skill, since the manager beat their net exposure
Poor performance, since the manager failed to beat the market
rationales: Absolute return says nothing about skill on its own. In a year the market rose 25%, +18% could have been achieved by an index fund at 70% exposure and cash at zero.

Correct. 70% net exposure into a 25% market gives roughly 0.70 x 25% = 17.5% from [[beta]] alone. The +18% actual leaves about 50 basis points of residual — indistinguishable from noise, and the investor paid hedge fund fees for it.
There is nothing to beat here: 18% versus the 17.5% that beta alone explains is not a meaningful margin, particularly before fees and financing costs.
Failing to beat the index is the wrong benchmark for a fund that deliberately runs 70% net exposure. Judging it against 100% of the market would penalise it for hedging, which is the opposite error.
questions.explanation: The right question is never "what was the return?" but "what was the return relative to the exposure taken?" Strip beta out first — what remains is the only part attributable to selection, and the only part worth a performance fee.

questions.stem: "Shorting a stock is simply the mirror image of buying it, with the profit and loss reversed." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — a short's loss is uncapped and the position grows as it moves against you, whereas a long's loss is capped and its position shrinks
False — shorting is prohibited for most hedge funds, so the comparison does not arise
True — the payoff is exactly symmetric, just with the sign flipped
False — because short positions do not require any capital to be committed
rationales: Correct. This asymmetry is mechanical, not a matter of opinion, and it drives real portfolio construction choices: short books are typically more diversified and more actively resized than long books.
Factually wrong — shorting is central to the strategy. Some *funds* have mandates that restrict it, but that is a constraint choice, not a prohibition on hedge funds.
This is the misconception under test. The payoff is not symmetric: a long can lose 100% at worst, while a short's potential loss has no ceiling.
Shorting very much requires capital — margin must be posted with the [[prime-broker]], and requirements can be raised. This is a separate misconception and also false.
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is the key structural fact about shorting. Losses compound into larger positions while gains shrink into smaller ones, which is why position sizing discipline matters more on the short side than pure idea quality.

questions.description: A fund's returns show a correlation of about 0.7 to global equities. It captures roughly 70% of the market's up moves and about 55% of its down moves. Gross exposure has averaged around 180% and net exposure has ranged between 40% and 75%. Its worst two months both occurred in *rising* markets, coinciding with sharp reversals in momentum and growth factors.
choices: Long/short equity, net long, with meaningful unintended factor exposure
Equity market neutral
Managed futures / CTA
Merger arbitrage
rationales: Correct. Persistent net long exposure of 40-75% and 0.7 correlation to equities are the signature. The telling detail is the worst months arriving in *rising* markets during factor reversals — that is the short book and an unintended [[factor-exposure]] failing together, not market risk.
[[equity-market-neutral]] would show net exposure near zero and correlation to equities close to zero. Capturing 70% of market upside is flatly inconsistent with being market neutral.
Managed futures typically show low or negative equity correlation and often profit in sustained equity declines. Consistently capturing 70% of equity upside is not that profile.
Merger arbitrage returns are driven by deal completion, producing low equity correlation with occasional sharp losses when deals break — not a smooth 0.7 correlation with high gross exposure.
questions.explanation: Two clues do most of the work. The asymmetric up/down capture with 0.7 correlation says persistent net long equity exposure. The worst months occurring in rising markets during factor reversals says the losses came from the short book and shared factor tilts — the characteristic long/short equity failure mode rather than a market event.

questions.stem: A manager's long book and short book both lose money in the same week, while the broad market is roughly flat. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: A short squeeze in a single position
A factor reversal, with the longs and shorts sharing an unintended factor tilt on opposite sides
Market beta, since net exposure was positive
Borrow costs rose sharply during the week
rationales: A squeeze in one name would hurt the short book, but it would not explain the long book losing simultaneously while the market is flat.

Correct. If the longs are concentrated in one factor and the shorts in its opposite, a reversal in that factor hits both legs at once. The flat market rules out beta, and simultaneous losses on both sides is the signature of a shared factor exposure.
A flat market means beta contributed roughly nothing. Beta cannot explain losses when the thing it is exposed to did not move.
Borrow costs are a real drag but far too small to explain a week of meaningful losses on both legs, and they would not affect the long book at all.
questions.explanation: Both legs losing while the market is flat is close to diagnostic of a shared factor exposure. It is also the most dangerous pattern in the strategy, because the manager believed they were hedged and the hedge turned out to be pointing the same way as the risk.

questions.stem: In diligence, a manager shows five years of strong returns but declines to break attribution out between the long and short books. Why does that specific gap matter most?
choices: Because attribution is required disclosure and refusing it signals a compliance problem
Because the returns could come entirely from the long book, making it an expensive long-only fund with a hedge that has destroyed value
Because without attribution you cannot compute gross exposure
Because short books are always the larger source of returns in this strategy
rationales: Attribution of this kind is not universally mandated disclosure, and framing it as a compliance issue misses the investment point — which is about what you are actually paying for.

Correct. This is a genuinely common pattern: a good long book paired with a short book that has lost money every year. The fund's total return can still look strong while the investor is paying hedge fund fees for something they could largely have bought as a long-only product.
Gross exposure comes from position-level long and short percentages, which are reported separately from performance attribution. You do not need attribution to compute it.
The reverse is more typical. Shorting is hard, and many long/short equity managers generate most of their gains on the long side.
questions.explanation: Long/short attribution answers the question the headline return cannot: which of the two things you are paying for is actually working? A short book that reliably loses money is not automatically fatal — it may be earning its keep as a risk reducer — but you need to see it and price it deliberately rather than discover it later.

questions.stem: During a stressed week, a manager running 250% gross faces a prime broker margin increase and a recall on several borrowed shares. Why is this combination especially dangerous?
choices: Because it forces the manager to trade in the direction that is already hurting them, at the worst possible prices
Because margin increases are always followed by fund closures
Because borrow recalls only affect the long book
Because high gross exposure protects against margin calls, so the recall must be a clerical error
rationales: Correct. The manager must sell longs and buy back shorts to reduce gross — precisely the trades that push their remaining positions further against them. At 250% gross, forced [[deleveraging]] moves a lot of stock, and if the trade is [[crowded-trade|crowded]], every other holder is doing the same thing at the same moment.
Overstated. Margin increases are routine in stressed markets and most funds handle them. The danger is the forced-selling mechanism, not an inevitability of failure.
Backwards. A borrow recall forces the closure of a *short* position — the manager must return the borrowed shares by buying them in the market.
High gross does the opposite: it makes a fund more vulnerable to margin increases, because more borrowed capacity is in use and there is less headroom.
questions.explanation: This is how a bad month becomes terminal. The mechanism is that stress removes the manager's choice about *when* to trade, and forced trades move prices against the remaining book. High gross exposure and crowded positioning are what turn a manageable loss into a spiral — which is why gross exposure and crowding, not just net exposure, belong in every risk conversation.
